metadata.title: Meta stock jumps 5% premarket: Analysts bullish on new Muse AI agent

content.text:
Investing.com -- Wall Street is greeting Meta Platforms' unveiling of "Muse" with broad optimism, framing the standalone personal AI agent as the tangible payoff investors have been demanding following quarters of aggressive artificial intelligence capital expenditure. That optimism quickly spilled over into Wednesday's trading; after a choppy initial reaction following the announcement, Meta shares jumped roughly 5% in pre-market action as investors digested the bullish analyst commentary.
Equity analysts across major firms broadly agree that the product marks the beginning of a major new product cycle—one that has yet to be fully priced into Meta's stock. Mizuho Securities analyst Lloyd Walmsley noted that investors have been eager to see a concrete return on Meta's massive infrastructure spending, calling Muse "a significant step in that direction" and pointing to the app's unexpected polish, broad functionality, and free entry price. Analysts at KeyBanc echoed that sentiment, maintaining a $780 price target and arguing that the market continues to "under-estimate Meta's AI positioning and product cycle."
A central theme among analysts is Meta's structural advantage in capturing what Morgan Stanley estimates to be a staggering $30 trillion total addressable market (TAM) for consumer agentic tasks across e-commerce, travel, digital ads, and daily logistics.
Morgan Stanley's Brian Nowak highlighted that winning this agentic battle requires two core ingredients: broad-based distribution and rich consumer datasets. Meta possesses both across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. When paired with intuitive privacy safeguards—like the dedicated Muse Secure VM—and zero upfront cost to consumers, Meta holds a distinct top-of-funnel edge over standalone AI startups.
However, analysts caution that Wall Street will not re-rate Meta's stock overnight. Because previous initiatives like Facebook Shopping and the Metaverse stumbled relative to high initial expectations, investors want hard data before pricing in long-term financial upside.
"As with other Meta apps, we view engagement as the initial barometer of success, with monetization following over time," noted KeyBanc's Justin Patterson. Nowak similarly stressed that while Muse represents one of the largest unpriced call options on Meta's long-term earnings, the market will need clear signals of user adoption and monetizable behavior before pushing shares structurally higher.
The launch also carries significant competitive implications for the broader tech landscape—most notably Alphabet. Analysts warn that if Muse successfully captures daily consumer intent for shopping, travel, and scheduling, it could siphon off valuable intent at the top of the funnel. As Morgan Stanley put it, a successful rollout for Muse "could pose a new potential threat to the position of search," elevating the stakes for Google to deliver strong innovation through its own Gemini pipeline.
